Berdoues
ber-DOO
n. (a Cistercian abbey in the Gers of Gascony, founded in the 1130s in the filiation of Morimond)
From the Gascon locality on the Gr ande Bais e; a local place name of uncertain derivation, probably from a stream or a green place.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Berdoues was founded in the 1130s in the valley of the Baïse in Gascony, in the Morimond line, and became the mother of further houses in the region, Gimont among them. Little of the abbey stands: the church was demolished after the Revolution and the site is partly a village and partly a garden. Its significance is as a mother house in a poor country — the Gascon abbeys were never rich, farmed thin land, and existed largely to settle and clear it. That makes Berdoues a good place to say something the romance of monasticism usually obscures: most of what these houses actually did was agriculture. The Cistercian granges drained, cleared, bred sheep and built mills, and they did it with lay brothers whose names nobody recorded. Scripture dignifies exactly that labour. “And the LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it” (Gen 2:15) puts work before the fall; “whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men” (Col 3:23) sanctifies it without a vow; and “that ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands” (1Th 4:11) is an apostolic command that describes a lay brother's day.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines agriculture as the cultivation of the ground for the purpose of producing vegetables and fruits for the use of man and beast; husbandry as the business of a farmer; and labor as exertion of muscular strength, toil, work.

expand to see more

AGRICULTURE, n. In a general sense, the cultivation of the ground, for the purpose of producing vegetables and fruits for the use of man and beast.

HUSBANDRY, n. The business of a farmer, comprehending agriculture or tillage of the ground, the raising, managing and fattening of cattle and other domestic animals.

LABOR, n. Exertion of muscular strength, or bodily exertion which occasions weariness; particularly, the exertion of the limbs in occupations by which subsistence is obtained.

TILL, v.t. To labor; to cultivate; to plow and prepare for seed, and to dress crops.

GRANGE, n. A farm, with the buildings, stables, etc.; a farm house with the adjoining buildings.

Key Scripture

Gen 2:15 — "And the LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it."

Col 3:23 — "And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men;"

1Th 4:11 — "And that ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands, as we commanded you;"

Pro 14:23 — "In all labour there is profit: but the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury."

Modern Corruption

A poor Gascon mother house of the 1130s, now mostly gone: a reminder that what these abbeys chiefly did was farm, with lay brothers whose names were never written down.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the dignity of ordinary labour. “In all labour there is profit: but the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury” (Pro 14:23) is blunt about which of the two a household lives on, and the Cistercian granges were a better argument for the order than its treatises were.

The live corruption, treated more fully under Opus Dei, is the two tiers the system built: the choir monk who prayed and the lay brother who dug, with the first counted the higher calling. “whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men” (Col 3:23) dissolves the ranking, and the men whose names were not recorded were doing God's work as fully as the men whose names were.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew abad (H5647), to work or serve; Hebrew adamah (H127), ground; Greek ergon (G2041), a work; Greek kopos (G2873), toil; Hebrew yagia (H3018), the labour of the hands.

expand to see more

Hebrew abad (H5647) — to work, till, serve; the same verb for farming and for worship.

Hebrew adamah (H127) — ground, soil; “to dress it and to keep it” (Gen 2:15).

Greek ergon (G2041) — a work or deed; the New Testament's common word for what a man does.

Greek kopos (G2873) — toil that wearies; “In all labour there is profit” (Pro 14:23) has the same realism.

Hebrew yagia (H3018) — toil, the produce of labour; what a grange actually yielded.

Usage

"“put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it” (Gen 2:15) — labour before the fall."

"“and to work with your own hands” (1Th 4:11) — an apostolic command, not a lesser calling."

"“In all labour there is profit” (Pro 14:23) — the economics of a Gascon grange."
